title: Sen. Jane M. Timken votes yea on SB423 to classify health care platform workers as independent contractors
text:
Sen. Jane M. Timken votes yea on SB423 to classify health care platform workers as independent contractors
K. L. Florez
State Sen. Jane M. Timken (R-29th) voted yea on SB423, a bill on the employment status of health care workers, which the Ohio Senate approved 33-0 on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, during the 136th Ohio General Assembly, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and include interpretation to clarify its provisions.
The bill states that, under specified conditions, health care workers who book shifts through an electronic health care worker platform are treated as independent contractors rather than employees of the platform or participating health care facilities. It defines key terms and sets out 15 criteria, such as freedom to accept or reject shifts, no minimum shift requirements, no noncompete clauses or hiring fees, lack of control over work methods, and responsibility for taxes and insurance. When those criteria are met, the worker is excluded from “employee” status for overtime, minimum wage, timely payment, workers’ compensation, unemployment, and state income tax withholding laws, with limited exceptions for existing W-2 employees and certain leave situations.
SB423 was introduced by Sen. Susan Manchester.
Timken was appointed to the Ohio State Senate to represent the 29th District and is currently the Republican National Committeewoman for Ohio.
She served as chairman of the Ohio Republican Party from 2017 to 2021, becoming the first woman elected to that position.
Timken graduated cum laude from Harvard College and received her J.D., summa cum laude, from American University, Washington College of Law. She began her legal career with the firm Black McCuskey and served as a magistrate and law clerk to the Honorable Judge Sara Lioi.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
